title: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI
pub: Pearls On, Gloves Off podcast, host Mary O'Carroll (Goodwin), YouTube
author: Shannon Thyme Klinger

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: Klinger directly supports the proposition with an operational example: contract-specific GPT self-service reportedly speeds responses and frees legal staff for more strategic, sophisticated work. st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Klinger accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI should selectively augment and reallocate work within a redesigned, human-led operating model rather than drive wholesale replacement. She materially extends it with an in-house implementation case: contract self-service, feedback loops and operational measurement reportedly reduced escalations and turnaround time, while freeing lawyers for strategic and ambiguous work. Her agentic claims are appropriately framed as forecasts rather than deployment evidence.
qs: Turnaround time is going from more than two weeks to just a couple of days.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Klinger supports the shift from lawyer-mediated tasks toward self-service and agentic delegation, including contract and e-discovery work within a secure enterprise environment. Her account provides a bounded current application and a forecast of further delegation, while not substantively addressing the cluster’s central cautions about error propagation, verification costs or intervention points.

kp.k: AI enablement targets workload rather than headcount reduction
kp.d: Klinger frames Moderna’s adoption as augmentation of a lean in-house team, not a cost-cutting or headcount-reduction programme. She says workload remains employees’ main complaint and argues that automating repetitive work creates capacity for strategic legal judgment. Her broader claim that AI will replace lawyers who fail to harness it is a prediction, not a reported employment outcome.
qs: I do not believe AI will replace lawyers. I do believe AI will replace those lawyers who don't learn how to harness AI to do even more and to drive even even greater impact.
We are not trying to replace people. We are not trying to reduce headcount.
Everyone's biggest complaint in our employee satisfaction surveys was workload and still is.

kp.k: Contract-specific GPTs move routine inquiries into business self-service
kp.d: Klinger reports that key contracts have dedicated GPTs accessible to business users, answering 90% of their questions. She contrasts this with lawyers retrieving agreements, searching provisions and composing responses. The stated benefits are faster turnaround and freeing lawyers for more complex work; the percentage is her operational account, not an independently presented accuracy study.
qs: the business has those GPTs where 90% of the questions they have are easily answered in the context of interacting with the GPT online

That frees the team up to be a lot more strategic in where they're playing up the curve of the complexity and sophistication of our business, but it also allows faster turnaround time when you think about that self-service.

kp.k: Contract facilitators handle transactions with fewer legal escalations
kp.d: Klinger says buy-side and sell-side contracting now runs through contract facilitators, with legal involved on escalation. AI monitors recurring negotiated changes to improve templates, while GPT-accessible playbooks reportedly answer 95% of facilitators’ questions. She reports average escalations across particular contract types falling from 15 to two and turnaround moving from more than two weeks to a couple of days, without supplying measurement periods or sample sizes. Escalations also arrive with more developed analysis and recommendations.
qs: those are all done now through contract facilitators with only legal escalations
the contract facilitators can actually just talk to the playbook through their GPT and get 95% of their questions answered.
you'd have 15 legal escalations on average across particular contract types. Those have been reduced to two. Turnaround time is going from more than two weeks to just a couple of days.
And then again, we put that into the feedback loop to be able to update templates.

kp.k: Enterprise confidentiality and sandbox experimentation underpin adoption
kp.d: Klinger describes legal’s involvement in an early OpenAI collaboration, when OpenAI did not yet have an enterprise instance. She identifies preventing proprietary information from training models as a prerequisite for business use, alongside sandbox experiments and continuing beta tests with business leaders and lawyers. Although the host raises hallucinations and downstream harm, Klinger’s response chiefly describes confidentiality safeguards and experimentation rather than a specified human-verification protocol.
qs: At the time, OpenAI had no enterprise instance.
We love your technology, but it will not work for businesses if we don't create the the ability not to have our information train your models.
it was only possible if the team was willing to experiment in a sandbox before you did things that created risk to talk about the risk, talk about the opportunity and find the right path forward.
there's a lot of beta tests in the background with the core group of business leaders.

kp.k: Contracting and discovery agents were anticipated by year-end
kp.d: Klinger expects legal operations leader Jeff to have two agents reporting to him by the end of the interview year, one in contracting and another in discovery. She envisages agents accessing information within a secure enterprise ecosystem and undertaking work otherwise assigned to a paralegal or Jeff. This is a prospective deployment claim, not confirmation that the agents were already operational.
qs: I expect by the end of this year he will have two agents reporting to him.
where you can use agents to crawl over and create pipelines into information in a secure enterprise ecosystem.
where they can be doing a lot of that work that before you'd task the parallegal with or Jeff would have to do himself.

kp.k: Experiential learning and failure tolerance support adoption
kp.d: Klinger describes a two-hour leadership exercise in which 12 initially sceptical participants explored use cases and learned to specify personas, problems, information sources and tone rather than treat AI as Google. She also reports mandatory workforce participation in an AI academy that began six to nine months before the OpenAI partnership. Her recommendation combines practical experimentation, leadership acceptance of imperfect results and repeated reassurance about employment intentions.
qs: we're going to spend two hours and we're just going to experiment with it.
I saw that mirrored back in 12 different people.
it wasn't because of what I was saying, it was because of what they were experiencing.
We had what is called an AI academy that started about six to nine months before we we entered the partnership with OpenAI.
failure is seen and rewarded because it is the best form of learning as opposed to something to be afraid of

kp.k: Regulatory monitoring and HR documentation become internal AI workflows
kp.d: Klinger describes an ESG tool built by the head of ESG strategy to track regulatory changes and compare requirements with the company’s position in real time, contrasting this with paying outside counsel for continuous monitoring 18 months earlier. Separately, an HR GPT standardises questions, captures answers and produces reports to improve documentation reliability and assist less-experienced investigators. These are qualitative accounts without quantified savings or reliability measurements.
qs: in the old world, and that's 18 months ago, just to show how fast things are going, in the old world, you'd have a law firm and you would pay the law firm sum of money to just constantly monitor the landscape and give you advice.
Our head of ESG strategy built that and now has the ability to track in real time what's happening.
compare it to where we are and be able to do gap analysis in real time
We created a GPT to allow our HR team in a very standard way to make sure they're asking the right questions, documenting the answer, putting that then into a report

kp.d: Klinger presents legal operations as a driver of efficiency and impact, freeing lawyers from administrative work. Her recommended sequence is to define the problem, map and improve the process, check stakeholders and approval levels, and only then apply AI. She explicitly rejects the premise that technology itself fixes inefficient workflows.
qs: legal operations as a as a driver of efficiency and impact for legal teams
we don't start with the technology. We actually start with mapping out the process.
Do we have the right stakeholders, people, things being approved at the right level?
Then I can put AI on top of it because AI is not going to fix an inefficient process. It's just going to curate that process differently.

kp.k: Internal transformation protects legal’s strategic position
kp.d: Klinger says early adoption was partly motivated by wanting the team to shape its own future rather than wait for Big Four consultants to propose disrupting legal to the CEO or chairman. She reports that the CEO recognised legal’s adoption on the Q1 2024 investor call and that her team now trains other functions. She recommends impact metrics, transparency about unsuccessful initiatives and running the legal function as a business to strengthen its relationship with senior leadership.
qs: Do I want to sit and wait for somebody in the big four consulting group to come to my chairman or my CEO and say we finally have figured out how to disrupt legal
Or did I want to control with our team and define our own destiny?
the Q1 call last year in 2024, legal gets called out by our CEO on our quarterly call.
if you have metrics that go to impact and not to your point metrics for the sake of metrics, what you're doing is running your function as a business

Her account positions lawyers as integrated business leaders, with active listening remaining important despite AI.

kp.k: Pricing and business models need ecosystem-wide redesign
kp.d: Klinger criticises discussion centred on savings, higher hourly rates and fee negotiations rather than relationships of value and impact. Her references to saving $5 million on a body of work and $4,000 hourly rates occur in a stylised account of the prevailing conversation, not a documented savings or pricing study. She identifies subscriptions to content usable by client GPTs as an opportunity and reports unspecified state-bar and confidentiality objections. O’Carroll separately argues that the harder challenge is redesigning recruitment, training, delivery, pricing and packaging, rather than AI itself.
qs: The conversation today is AI is allowing me to save $5 million on a particular body of work.
we love the hourly rate and now we're going to be $4,000 an hour
We don't want to do subscription services for content over which we can crawl our own GPTs. Some under the state bars don't let us.
And I think that's gotten lost in the abject feebased negotiations.

The hard part is figuring out the business model and what needs to change fundamentally about how we retain, attract, train lawyers and how do we deliver legal services and price and package it in a way that is client focused.

kp.k: Practitioner knowledge-sharing supports collective AI capability
kp.d: Klinger describes an Association of Corporate Counsel AI centre of excellence launching on the interview day, intended as a practitioner community for lawyers and legal operations professionals to exchange current information, use cases and prompts. She frames it as a response to fragmented bilateral activity and the abundance of vendors, recommending collective learning rather than isolated adoption.
qs: At some point today, we are launching on ACC's website an AI center of excellence.
an opportunity to really put in one place what's current, but actually then exchange use cases and prompts and just a place to really create an interactive community.
There's a lot of vendors out there. There's a lot of people doing things bilaterally, but again, we can become better together as a community.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shannon Thyme Klinger describes AI as already transferring routine legal work to business self-service, improving contracting and bringing sophisticated drafting in-house; she predicts changes to legal work, training and career pathways rather than straightforward elimination of lawyers.
pts.d: Klinger makes the following claims. (1) Lawyers who do not learn to harness AI will be replaced, while AI-enabled lawyers can increase their impact. At Moderna, she expressly frames adoption as workload relief and strategic redeployment, not headcount reduction. (2) Contract-specific GPTs answer approximately 90% of business users' questions about key contracts, replacing document retrieval and explanatory emails by legal staff. (3) Across buy-side and sell-side contracting, AI-supported templates and playbooks enable contract facilitators to handle work with legal involvement principally through escalations. She reports that GPT-enabled playbooks answer 95% of facilitators' questions, average legal escalations across particular contract types have fallen from 15 to two, and turnaround has shortened from more than two weeks to a couple of days. AI also identifies recurring negotiated changes that can be incorporated into templates, while escalations arrive with more focused recommendations. (4) She expects the legal operations leader to have two AI agents, in contracting and e-discovery, performing information-access and workflow tasks previously assigned to him or a paralegal. (5) She describes an ESG GPT as enabling real-time regulatory monitoring and gap analysis, work previously purchased from a law firm. She also describes an HR GPT that standardizes questions, answers and reports, improving documentation reliability and supporting less-experienced investigators. Separately, she says CDAs are automated through another GPT. (6) AI supplies assistance analogous to a coach or junior associate, enabling lawyers with three to five years' experience to undertake more advanced work. (7) AI-enabled internal teams now prepare more first drafts of sophisticated transactional and licensing agreements, then request targeted outside-counsel review. Klinger says this creates efficiency and cost savings but transfers mid-to-senior associate work away from firms, eroding work that historically trained lawyers. (8) She predicts a possible reversal of the traditional career pipeline: more graduates could start in-house, learn business law with technological support and increased teaching by legal leaders, and later move to law firms with industry expertise. (9) She warns that AI could disrupt or partly disintermediate legal departments and the profession. Early internal adoption allows legal teams to shape that change instead of waiting for a Big Four consulting group to propose restructuring to corporate leadership. (10) She argues that in-house teams and firms must jointly redesign training and value delivery. She presents subscriptions to content accessible by clients' GPTs as a missed opportunity, contrasts this with escalating hourly rates, and anticipates change in some constraints on such offerings. Failure to adapt could leave the profession substantially different in ten years. These are Klinger's claims; the host's parallel views about pricing and business models are not treated as evidence for them.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is chiefly Klinger's first-hand account of Moderna's implementations, including selected internal performance figures; the wider employment, career-pipeline and market claims are predictions rather than demonstrated findings.
pts.d: For self-service and contracting, Klinger supplies numerical internal results: 90% of key-contract questions answered through GPT interaction, 95% of facilitator questions answered through playbooks, escalations falling from 15 to two, and turnaround falling from over two weeks to a couple of days. She says the team tracks impact, but provides no underlying dataset, sample size, measurement period, definition of a successfully answered question, or independent assessment. The question-answer percentages are not presented as model-accuracy benchmarks or hallucination-rate measurements. Her qualitative evidence consists of descriptions of more sophisticated escalations, template feedback loops, an ESG monitoring tool built by the head of ESG strategy, an HR documentation tool, CDA automation, and targeted external review of internally drafted deals. Her claim that relatively junior lawyers can do more advanced work rests on her observations of her team, not comparative performance testing. The adoption argument is supported by an anecdote about a two-hour leadership experiment in which initially skeptical participants identified useful applications, together with mandatory workforce AI education. She reports that Moderna is lean against staffing benchmarks and that employee surveys identify workload as a major concern, without naming the benchmark or providing survey data. She also cites CEO recognition of legal's adoption on a Q1 2024 investor call as evidence of organizational recognition, not a quantified productivity result. Her expectation of two agents, possible reverse career migration, and ten-year professional transformation are forward-looking judgments. The Big Four example is a hypothetical competitive threat, not an account of an actual engagement. The $5 million savings and $4,000 hourly rate language appears in a stylized description of current industry conversations, rather than a documented Moderna savings case or verified rate survey. No specific state rule or legal authority is identified for the asserted barriers to content subscriptions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most operational changes are described as already implemented by the 2025 interview; agents are expected by year-end, while career reversal is tentative and the broader warning has a ten-year horizon. Benefits depend on secure deployment, redesigned processes, experimentation and additional human teaching.
pts.d: The document dates the interview to 2025. Klinger describes contract self-service, facilitator-led contracting, HR documentation, CDA automation and AI-assisted transactional drafting as current practices. She contrasts current ESG monitoring with the outside-law-firm model of approximately 18 months earlier. The two agents are an expectation for the end of the interview year, not a completed deployment. She characterizes the technology as having advanced rapidly over the preceding two years and describes Moderna's early collaboration with OpenAI as beginning before an enterprise instance was available. She says workforce AI education began six to nine months before that partnership. Conditions for adoption include protecting confidential information, preventing company information from training provider models, experimenting in a sandbox before exposing the business to risk, and beta testing new capabilities with a core group that includes lawyers. Her assurance about secure agent access is a deployment intention, not a reported security test. She emphasizes first mapping and improving the process: AI will not itself fix inefficiency. Practical experimentation, clear problem definition, training, trust and repeated reassurance that the goal is enablement support adoption. The work-allocation model is mixed: routine questions and transactions move toward business self-service, while difficult issues escalate to lawyers and sophisticated drafts receive targeted outside-counsel review. She does not specify a universal human-verification requirement or measured hallucination controls. Reverse migration is explicitly speculative and would require more teaching by in-house leadership. The ten-year warning is conditional on the profession failing to redesign its relationships, training and value proposition. Her opening rejection of wholesale lawyer replacement coexists with a later warning that the profession itself could be displaced if it fails to respond.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern a corporate legal department and its business users; the wider implications concern outside firms' work and revenue, associate training, legal operations responsibilities and entry routes into the profession.
pts.d: Moderna's in-house lawyers are described as gaining capacity for strategic, complex and ambiguous issues rather than being targeted for layoffs. Business users obtain faster answers without routinely routing questions through legal. Procurement and sell-side contract facilitators take on more contracting with GPT-supported playbooks, escalating fewer and more focused issues. Legal operations gains responsibility for configuring and overseeing AI-supported workflows and potentially agents, while tasks traditionally performed by an operations leader or paralegal become candidates for automation; this is not evidence that a named paralegal was dismissed. HR and ESG personnel gain tools for standardized documentation, investigations, monitoring and gap analysis. Younger in-house lawyers contribute strongly to tool development and may undertake more sophisticated work with AI assistance. Outside counsel face reduced demand for routine regulatory monitoring and first-draft transactional work, with more narrowly scoped review requests replacing some larger assignments. Associates face a potential loss of work-based training; law firms and in-house leaders are asked to share responsibility for creating replacement learning pathways. Graduates could have more direct in-house entry opportunities, and experienced in-house lawyers might later join firms with business and industry knowledge. CLOs and legal operations professionals are positioned as organizational transformation leaders, with greater responsibility for process design, data and teaching. The Big Four appear as hypothetical competitors for control over legal-function redesign, not as legal-tech vendors or documented providers in this account. The claimed benefits are principally enterprise service improvements and cost or capacity gains; the source does not supply an access-to-justice claim about unmet civil legal need.
